results.result: UPEC bacteria were found in all epididymal regions 1 day post infection, persisted at high numbers only in the cauda for up to 10 days, and are cleared by day 30.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 describe the experimental model and bacterial kinetics. C1 describes the experimental procedure, C2-C3 are supported by bacterial load measurements (Figure 1B), and C4 is supported by citation to prior work. The bacterial distribution and persistence data are clearly documented.

results.result: The caput showed minimal histopathological changes following UPEC infection, with slight alterations at 5 days that resolved by 10 days post infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 are supported by histological data (Figure 1C) and disease score measurements (Figure 1D). The transient nature of the response in the caput is well-documented and corroborated by prior work (Klein et al., 2020).

results.result: The cauda exhibited severe tissue remodeling following UPEC infection, characterized by immune cell infiltration, loss of epithelial integrity, connective tissue deposition, and persistent elevated disease scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by extensive histological data (Figure 1E, supplemental figures) and disease score measurements (Figure 1F). The progressive nature of pathology from peripheral to widespread is documented. This is corroborated by prior work (Klein et al., 2020).

results.result: Sham control mice showed mild histopathological alterations in the cauda that resolved by day 10 post infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by histological data (Figure 1E, 1F, supplemental figures). This demonstrates that surgical trauma alone causes transient inflammation that resolves, distinguishing it from UPEC-induced pathology.

results.result: RNAseq analysis revealed minimal transcriptional changes in the caput (5 DEGs) but extensive changes in the cauda (5082 DEGs) between sham and UPEC-infected mice, with the corpus showing intermediate changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by RNAseq data (Figure 1G, supplemental figures) with clearly defined statistical cutoffs (FDR ≤0.05, |logFC| > 1). The PCA analysis (Figure 1 supplement 3A) supports the intermediate position of the corpus. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3-4 per group).

results.result: The caput was highly enriched in transcripts encoding immunomodulatory factors (β-defensins, bactericidal permeability-increasing protein, indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1) with no changes between sham and UPEC-infected mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by RNAseq data (Figure 1H). The constitutive high expression of immunomodulatory factors in the caput regardless of infection status is clearly shown and suggests a baseline immunoregulatory environment.

results.result: The cauda of UPEC-infected mice showed upregulation of pro-inflammatory mediators and gene sets associated with fibrotic tissue remodeling and pro-inflammatory immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by RNAseq data (Figure 1H, supplemental figures) and gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 1I). The specific genes and pathways mentioned are documented, and the analysis methods appear appropriate.

results.result: Pathway analyses revealed upregulation of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation in the cauda at 10 days post infection, indicating a transition from innate to adaptive immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 are supported by pathway analysis (Figure 1 supplement 3). C22 is an interpretation of C21, but it is a reasonable inference given the timing (10 days) and the specific gene sets identified. This is further corroborated by flow cytometry data showing increased B and T cells (C36-C37).

results.result: The caput was enriched with gene sets related to sperm maturation, indicative of normal epididymal function.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 1I). C24 is an interpretation of C23, but it is reasonable given that sperm maturation is a primary function of the caput. The maintenance of these gene sets in both sham and infected mice supports the interpretation of preserved function.

results.result: Disease progression correlated with immune cell infiltration in the cauda. Sham mice showed transient immune cell increases peaking at day 5 and resolving by day 14, attributed to surgical trauma.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2A, 2B) and correlation analysis. C28 is an interpretation, but it is reasonable given that sham mice (surgery without bacteria) show transient inflammation that resolves. The correlation between disease score and immune infiltration is statistically supported.

results.result: UPEC infection caused increased immune cell infiltration in the cauda, with the caput showing significant increases only at day 14. Infiltration peaked at 10 days and correlated with disease score.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2B, 2C). The regional differences and temporal dynamics are clearly documented. The correlation between infiltration and disease score is statistically supported (Figure 2C).

results.result: CX3CR1+ macrophages dominated in the IS and caput, while the corpus and cauda showed more diverse immune cell composition. Neutrophils and monocytes infiltrated primarily the corpus and cauda upon UPEC infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 2D-F, supplemental figures). The regional differences in immune cell composition are clearly documented. The absence of neutrophils in naive mice and their appearance upon infection is well-supported.

results.result: Both corpus and cauda showed significant increases in B and T lymphocytes after sham injection and UPEC infection, correlating with gene set enrichment for B and T cell activation at 10 days post infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2G) and correlation with gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 1 supplement 3E). The multi-modal evidence (protein and RNA levels) strengthens the conclusion about adaptive immune response activation.

results.result: The ratio of CX3CR1+ macrophages decreased in infected mice, particularly in proximal regions. In distal regions, this was accompanied by increased CX3CR1- macrophages and CCR2+ cells, indicating monocyte contribution to the macrophage pool.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2G, 2H). C39 and C41 are interpretations, but they are reasonable given the known biology of CCR2+ monocytes and their differentiation into macrophages. The regional differences are clearly documented.

results.result: The corpus and cauda developed a highly inflammatory immune environment with co-existing myeloid and lymphoid cells. Sham-infected mice showed similar but milder changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 are summary interpretations supported by the flow cytometry data in Figure 2D-H. The characterization of the immune environment is consistent with the detailed cellular composition data. The comparison with sham mice is well-documented.

results.result: Ly6G+ and Ly6C+ cells (neutrophils and monocytes) progressively increased in the cauda interstitium and were found in the epithelium when epithelial integrity was disturbed.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2I). The spatial localization and temporal dynamics are clearly documented. The association with epithelial damage is consistent with the histological observations.

results.result: Ex vivo LPS stimulation showed that IS and caput were mostly unreactive while corpus and cauda showed significant cytokine upregulation. IS and caput showed higher intracellular bacterial loads, suggesting higher bacterial uptake and clearance potential. These differences are inherent to the regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by ex vivo cytokine measurements (Figure 2 supplement 3A) and gentamicin assay data (Figure 2 supplement 3B). C48 and C49 are interpretations, but they are reasonable. The ex vivo approach controls for bacterial exposure route, supporting the conclusion that regional differences are intrinsic. However, the gentamicin assay interpretation (C48) requires caution as higher intracellular bacteria could also reflect different epithelial permeability or bacterial invasion mechanisms rather than solely clearance capacity.

results.result: scRNASeq analysis of 12,966 CD45+ cells from four epididymal regions identified 13 distinct clusters, including macrophage, monocyte, dendritic cell, and lymphocyte subsets, characterized by specific marker gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 describe the scRNASeq experimental design and cluster identification. The data are supported by UMAP plots (Figure 3B), gene expression heatmaps (Figure 3C), and marker gene expression (Figure 3D-E). The cell numbers and cluster identification appear robust. The marker genes used for cell type identification are appropriate and well-established.

results.result: Flow cytometry validation showed that the IS contained the highest proportion of resident immune cells (10-15% CD45+), predominantly macrophages (78% in IS, 66% in caput). The corpus and cauda contained more heterogeneous immune cell populations with lower macrophage proportions (25-35%) and higher proportions of monocytes (7-10%) and dendritic cells (cDC1: 7-10%, cDC2: 12-20%).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 4A-E) and immunofluorescence analysis. The quantification is clear and the regional differences are well-documented. The validation of scRNASeq findings by flow cytometry strengthens the conclusions. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=4-8).

results.result: No plasmacytoid dendritic cells were found in the murine epididymis. Lymphocyte subsets (NK cells, B cells, T cells including αβ and γδ T cells) were located in both interstitial and intraepithelial compartments, with γδ T cells specifically found within the epithelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data (Figure 4F-H). C66 is corroborated by prior work (Voisin et al., 2018). The spatial localization of lymphocyte subsets is clearly documented.

results.result: The proximal and distal regions showed striking differences in their immunological landscapes, with resident immune cells strategically positioned to address contrasting immunological challenges.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are summary conclusions supported by the comprehensive immune cell characterization data (Figures 3-4). The interpretation that strategic positioning addresses different challenges is reasonable given the functional differences between proximal (sperm maturation) and distal (pathogen entry) regions, though it remains somewhat speculative about the specific functional roles.

results.result: Macrophages (Adgre1+C1qa+) constitute the majority of CD45+ cells. Macrophage populations (clusters 1, 2, 7) were distinguished from monocyte populations (clusters 8, 10) based on differential expression of C1qa, Ccr2, Ly6c2, Napsa, and Plac8. Cluster 10 represents classical monocytes while cluster 8 represents monocytes differentiating into macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by scRNASeq data (Figure 5A, Figure 3D). C71 is corroborated by citation to Dick et al., 2022. C75 is an interpretation based on intermediate marker expression (C76), which is reasonable given the known biology of monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation. The gene expression patterns support the cell type assignments.

results.result: Re-clustering of macrophage populations identified nine subgroups with distinct gene expression profiles. Clusters 1 and 2, the majority of macrophages, expressed genes associated with homeostatic and sensing functions similar to brain microglia, including Cx3cr1, Tmem119, P2ry12, P2ry13, Gpr34, Rnase4, Olfml3, and Tgfbr1.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by re-clustering analysis (Figure 5B-E). C80 is an inference based on gene expression similarity to macrophages in other tissues, which is reasonable but should be validated functionally. The gene expression data are clearly presented and the comparison to brain microglia is supported by appropriate citations (Hickman et al., 2013; Van Hove et al., 2019; Abels et al., 2021).

results.result: Cluster 2 expressed high levels of MHC-II transcripts indicating an activated status for antigen presentation. Cluster 6 showed similar expression to cluster 2 but was enriched with cytokines, chemokines, and immediate-early response genes, likely representing an activated form of cluster 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 5C-D, supplemental figures). C82 and C85 are interpretations that are reasonable given the gene expression patterns. C84 appropriately acknowledges that immediate-early response genes could be artifacts of tissue processing (Denisenko et al., 2020), which is an important caveat.

results.result: Clusters 3 and 4 were enriched with Ccr2 and MHC-II transcripts indicating an activated pro-inflammatory phenotype. Cluster 3 expressed high levels of activation genes including immediate-early response genes and cytokines/chemokines, representing an activated subset of cluster 4.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 5C-D, supplemental figures). C86 and C88 are interpretations that are reasonable given the gene expression patterns. The grouping of clusters 3 and 4 as one subgroup is justified by their transcriptional similarity.

results.result: Clusters 5 and 9 were enriched with Cd163, Lyve1, and Folr2 but showed reciprocal expression of Timd4 and Ccr2, indicating similar anti-inflammatory or regulatory phenotypes but different ontogenies.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 5D, supplemental figures). C90 is an interpretation that is reasonable given the reciprocal expression of ontogeny markers (Timd4 for embryonic-derived, Ccr2 for monocyte-derived). This interpretation is further validated by the parabiosis experiments (C121-C122).

results.result: Clusters 7 and 8 were minor subgroups with low expression of Ccr2, Cd163, Lyve1, Timd4, and Cx3cr1. Cluster 7 expressed Trem2 and MHC-II transcripts, while cluster 8 showed high expression of Adgre1 and Acp5.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 5D). The characterization of these minor populations is clear, though their functional significance remains to be determined.

results.result: The most striking difference among macrophage subpopulations was their differential distribution among epididymal regions. Seven macrophage subpopulations were distinguished based on transcriptional profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by regional distribution analysis (Figure 5F) and the overall scRNASeq analysis. The summary of seven subpopulations (grouping activated clusters with their parent clusters) is reasonable and facilitates interpretation.

results.result: F4/80+ cells constituted approximately 80% of CD45+ cells in the IS, decreasing to 25% in the cauda. These cells were found in both epithelial and interstitial compartments and were predominantly CX3CR1+, with a small fraction of intraepithelial CX3CR1+ cells being F4/80- in the IS.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6A-C, supplemental figures) and immunofluorescence analysis. The quantification is clear and the regional gradient is well-documented. The identification of a small F4/80-CX3CR1+ population in the IS is interesting and warrants further investigation.

results.result: CX3CR1+CCR2-MHC-II- (cluster 1) and CX3CR1+CCR2-MHC-II+ (clusters 2 and 6) macrophages were highly abundant in the IS (40% each of F4/80+ cells). Both declined toward the cauda, though the ratio of CX3CR1+CCR2-MHC-II+ cells remained similar across regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6B, supplemental figures). The validation of scRNASeq findings by flow cytometry is appropriate. The regional distribution patterns are clearly documented.

results.result: CX3CR1+CCR2-MHC-II- macrophages (cluster 1) were located within the epididymal epithelium. Intraepithelial macrophages in the IS exhibited long protrusions toward the lumen and did not express MHC-II, but gained MHC-II expression in caput, corpus, and cauda. CX3CR1+CCR2-MHC-II+ cells (clusters 2 and 6) closely surrounded the epididymal duct with highest density in the IS.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6C-D, supplemental figures). The spatial localization and morphological features are clearly documented. The gain of MHC-II expression in more distal regions is an interesting observation that suggests regional functional differences.

results.result: CX3CR1+CCR2+MHC-II+ macrophages (clusters 3 and 4) were less abundant in the IS and caput (5-10%) but constituted 20-30% of macrophages in the corpus and cauda. These triple positive macrophages were localized exclusively in the interstitium, most prominently in the cauda.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6B) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 6D, supplemental figures). The opposite distribution pattern compared to clusters 1 and 2 is clearly documented and consistent with the scRNASeq data.

results.result: CD163+CCR2- macrophages (cluster 5) constituted 3-10% of resident macrophages, predominantly in the corpus. CD163+CCR2+ macrophages (cluster 9) were most abundant in the corpus and cauda (10% of F4/80+ cells). CD163 single positive cells were clustered near vascular structures and appeared smaller than solitarily distributed CD163+CCR2+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6B, supplemental figures) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 6E). The spatial localization near vasculature for CD163+ cells is consistent with their known biology as vasculature-associated macrophages.

results.result: F4/80+CX3CR1-CCR2-CD163- cells were considered to be macrophages of clusters 7 and 8, with cluster 7 expressing MHC-II. Both were most abundant in the corpus but constituted only 1-4% of total CD45+ cells and were exclusively found in the interstitium.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 6B, supplemental figures) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 6D, supplemental figures). C112 is an inference based on the gating strategy and scRNASeq cluster identification, which is reasonable. These minor populations are well-characterized despite their low abundance.

results.result: The regional and compartmental distribution suggests that distinct macrophage subsets populate the epididymis to facilitate different functions: 'scavenger functions' in the epithelial compartment of proximal regions to maintain tissue integrity, and 'guardian functions' in distal regions to tackle invading pathogens and tissue regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are summary interpretations of the macrophage distribution data. While the distribution patterns are well-documented, the functional assignments ('scavenger' vs 'guardian') are speculative and based on inference from location and marker expression rather than direct functional assays. The interpretations are reasonable but would benefit from functional validation.

results.result: Parabiosis experiments between CD45.1+ wild type and CD45.2+ Ccr2-/- mice for 6 months showed efficient chimerism (40-60% of blood Ly6Chi cells from donor). All CCR2+ cells (clusters 3, 4, 9) were exclusively of donor origin, while TIMD4+ cells (cluster 5) were not donor-derived. The majority of macrophages were CCR2-TIMD4- double negative.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C124 are supported by parabiosis experimental data (Figure 7A-H, supplemental figures). The experimental design is appropriate for assessing monocyte contribution to tissue macrophages. The 6-month duration is sufficient for steady-state analysis. C124 is an inference based on the gating strategy, which is reasonable.

results.result: Double negative epididymal macrophages were generally less monocyte-dependent than epididymal fat macrophages. Significant regional differences were detected: CCR2-TIMD4- macrophages in IS and caput had very low donor chimerism (5-10% normalized to blood), while those in corpus and cauda showed much higher chimerism (30-40% normalized to blood).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are supported by chimerism analysis from the parabiosis experiment (Figure 7C, 7I). The normalization to blood chimerism is appropriate. The regional differences in monocyte-dependence are clearly documented and statistically significant. Sample size (n=6) is adequate for parabiosis experiments.

results.result: The parabiosis data indicate a higher monocyte-dependent turnover rate of resident macrophages in the distal epididymis (corpus and cauda) but only a minor impact of monocytes in maintaining macrophages in the proximal regions (IS and caput).
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 are interpretations of the parabiosis chimerism data that are well-supported. The conclusions are consistent with the observed chimerism patterns and the known biology of macrophage ontogeny. The interpretation that distal regions, where pathogens enter first, have higher monocyte-dependent turnover is logical.

results.result: Immunopathological damage following UPEC infection occurs almost exclusively in the cauda epididymidis with loss of epithelial integrity, interstitial fibrosis, and duct obstruction. The leukocytic infiltration is characterized by a massive influx of neutrophils and monocyte-derived MHC-IIhi macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 are supported by the current study's histological and flow cytometry data and corroborated by citations to prior work (Michel et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2020). The characterization of the immune infiltrate is well-documented.

results.result: Neutrophils and monocyte-derived macrophages are important first defenders during acute infection but can also cause collateral tissue injury. Ccr2-/- mice show reduced influx of these cells and less severe tissue damage, indicating they act as double-edged swords in acute epididymitis.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 are supported by established knowledge (C133) and citations to relevant literature (C134: Segel et al., 2011; Kruger et al., 2015; C135-C136: Wang et al., 2021). The interpretation of a 'double-edged sword' role is reasonable and well-supported by the cited evidence.

results.result: Bacterial virulence factors may contribute to tissue damage in the cauda given that UPEC persist longer and at higher numbers in this region. Extravasation of immunogenic spermatozoa through the damaged epithelial barrier may trigger an adaptive immune response against spermatozoal neo-antigens.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 are speculations about mechanisms of persisting immunopathology. While they are reasonable hypotheses based on the observed bacterial persistence and epithelial damage, they lack direct experimental support in this study. These are appropriate as discussion points but should not be considered established findings.

results.result: Granulomas can be induced by interstitial sperm injection alone, leading to massive tissue destruction in the cauda. Formation of anti-sperm antibodies is seen in E. coli-elicited epididymitis models and in epididymitis patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 are supported by citations to relevant literature (C139: Itoh et al., 1999; C140: Ingerslev et al., 1986; Nashan et al., 1993; Lotti et al., 2018; Silva et al., 2021). These claims provide context for the potential role of sperm antigens in persisting immunopathology.

results.result: The upregulation of S100a9 within the caput could drive macrophages to polarize to an anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive phenotype as seen in the testis following UPEC infection.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 is a speculation based on findings from Fan et al., 2021 in the testis. While S100a9 upregulation is observed in the caput, the functional consequence on macrophage polarization is not directly tested in this study. This is an appropriate hypothesis for future investigation but lacks direct support.

results.result: The data unravel the transcriptional identity and tissue location of extravascular immune cells and support the existence of distinct immunological environments along the epididymal duct. The transcriptional profile of intraepithelial CX3CR1+ cells combined with known phagocytic potential indicates a central function in tissue homeostasis and immune surveillance.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 are summary conclusions supported by the comprehensive characterization of immune cells. C143 is an interpretation based on transcriptional profile data and supported by citations to prior functional studies (Smith et al., 2014; Battistone et al., 2020). The interpretation is reasonable though functional validation in this specific context would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The high density of sensing CX3CR1hi macrophages in combination with the narrow lumen of the IS indicates a potential function of this region as an 'immunological bottleneck' to monitor luminal content, induce tolerance toward sperm antigens, and eliminate pathogens.
results.evaluation: Claim C144 is a speculation based on macrophage distribution and anatomical features. While the 'immunological bottleneck' concept is an interesting hypothesis consistent with the data, it lacks direct functional validation. This is appropriate as a discussion point but should not be considered an established finding.

results.result: The co-existence of antigen-presenting myeloid cells with lymphocyte subtypes in distal regions implies an environment of immune responsiveness. The existence of innate-like lymphocytes (NK cells, γδ T cells) implies their contribution to immune responses against pathogens. Their function depends on activation status and local environmental factors may determine regulatory vs. cytotoxic functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 are interpretations of the immune cell composition data. C145-C146 are reasonable inferences from the cell distribution data. C147-C148 are supported by citations to relevant literature (Shi et al., 2011; Papotto et al., 2017; Bonneville et al., 2010; Klose and Artis, 2020). C149 is a speculation but is reasonable given the known biology of innate lymphoid cells.

results.result: The scRNASeq approach provides a snapshot of immune cells at a defined time, which is a limitation. The data provide the first atlas of extravascular CD45+ cells in the murine epididymis under normal conditions. Strategic positioning of immune cells strongly indicates the existence of distinct immunological landscapes that drive differences in immune responsiveness upon bacterial infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 are summary statements. C150 appropriately acknowledges a limitation of the study. C151 is a factual statement about the study's contribution. C152-C153 are conclusions drawn from the comprehensive immune cell characterization data. The conclusions are well-supported by the data, though the causal link between immune cell positioning and differential immune responsiveness (C153) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.
